title.goal: Set the promise: one Jakarta EE service, made faster, then broken, then fixed.

clicks.say: “I’m Bazlur. In the next 45 minutes we take one Jakarta EE service, switch it to virtual threads with one line, and watch it get faster. Then we give it a bigger day and watch it break. Then we fix it by writing down limits we never knew we had.”
clicks.tip: Press T so your real time shows on the ruler. In a second terminal, have ./run.sh db, provider and app already running.

hands.goal: Find out who runs virtual threads, and plant the question the talk answers.

clicks.say: “Quick poll in the chat. Type 1 if you run Java 21 or later in production.”
clicks.tip: Give the chat ten seconds. Read a few answers out.

clicks.say: “Type 2 if virtual threads are switched on.”
“And type 3 if you changed anything else when you switched them on. That last one is this talk.”

one-line.goal: Switching them on is trivial. The consequences are not in the diff.

clicks.say: “In Jakarta EE 11, Jakarta Concurrency 3.1 lets a managed executor run on virtual threads. It is one attribute: virtual = true.”
“Java 21 or later, and a Jakarta EE 11 server with Concurrency 3.1: Web Profile or the full platform. I use Open Liberty today, but nothing here is Liberty-specific until I say so.”
“Nothing in this diff looks like a bug in code review. Keep that in mind.”

plan.goal: Give the map of the talk.

clicks.say: “The plan. First a small sale: sixteen platform threads struggle, virtual threads fix it.”
“Then the launch: a big sale, 700 reservations a second. That is where it breaks.”
“Then we rebuild it, writing the limits down.”
“And last, deadlines: what happens to the work after the customer gives up.”
“Every number you see was measured on this laptop with k6. Nothing is drawn by hand.”

platform.goal: Show what a waiting platform thread costs, so the audience sees what virtual threads change.

clicks.say: “A platform thread is a thin wrapper around an operating-system thread. One task takes one thread and keeps it until it finishes.”
clicks.tip: Point at one lane: the request on the left, its work drawn to the right.

clicks.say: “The solid part is real work. The hatched part is waiting for the database, and for a typical service that is most of the time. The thread is held the whole time.”
clicks.more: About a megabyte of stack is reserved per thread. The real cost is that OS threads are limited, so every server caps them.

clicks.say: “Because threads are expensive we pool them. In our service the pool is sixteen. Remember that number: it was quietly doing a second job.”

virtual.goal: Mount, park, unmount: the one mechanism the rest of the talk relies on.

clicks.say: “A virtual thread is a thread the JVM schedules itself. It needs an OS thread, its carrier, only while it is running.”
“When it blocks, on a socket, a sleep or a lock, the JVM parks it and the carrier picks up another one. Nobody holds an OS thread while waiting.”
“When the answer comes, it mounts again on whichever carrier is free. Your code is still plain blocking code.”
“So thousands can wait at once on a few carriers. The advice is: never pool virtual threads. Hold on to that advice. It is about to cost us.”

intro-race.goal: The gain is throughput. No single request got faster.

clicks.say: “A measurement from my last talk, in plain Java: a thousand requests, each waits 100 ms. Top lane, a pool of 50. Bottom lane, a thread each.”
Let it play. “Fifty at a time on top. Everyone else queues for a thread.”
“2,084 milliseconds against 114. But every request still waited its 100 ms. Nothing got faster. We stopped queueing for a thread.”

service.goal: Show the service and every limit in it, before anything breaks.

clicks.say: “This is the service. One reservation holds four seats and charges one card, and it does all five at once on a managed executor.”
clicks.tip: Start ./run.sh watch in the second terminal now if it is not running.

clicks.say: “The seat holds go through a pool of 20 database connections, about 10 ms each. The payment goes to a provider that takes 20 charges at a time, 50 ms each. Above 20 it says no: HTTP 429. Two things are simulated, and I want to say so: the 10 ms is a pg_sleep in the query, and the provider is a small fake that sleeps 50 ms. Everything else is real Liberty, real PostgreSQL and real k6.”
“The executor has sixteen platform threads. Somebody chose sixteen years ago.”
“And the payment call has @Retry on it, the MicroProfile defaults. So far the provider has never said no, so it has never fired.”

before-run.goal: Run the small sale live on platform threads.

clicks.say: “A small sale. 60 reservations a second, then 120 more a second for six seconds.”
“Watch p99 on the k6 dashboard.”
clicks.tip: Expect p99 around one second during the sale and about 700 late. If the live run misbehaves, open results/before-small-7.html.

clicks.say: “So we do what everyone does. We switch to virtual threads.”
“And we follow the advice: never pool virtual threads. So maxAsync = 16 goes, and virtual = true comes in.”
“Same small sale.”
clicks.tip: First ./run.sh state switched; liberty:dev reloads in about a second. Fallback: results/switched-small-7.html.

clicks.say: Plays the platform-thread run. “These charts are the recorded rehearsal runs, so your live numbers just now will be close, not identical. Sixteen threads: p99 a second during the sale. The executor is the queue.”
Plays the virtual-thread run over it. “Virtual threads: 72 milliseconds. Same sale. Faster. This is the slide everyone shows.”

big-ask.goal: Set up the climax and ask for a prediction.

clicks.say: “Now the launch. 700 a second, for three seconds. The same service, the same switch.”
“What happens to p99? Type your guess in the chat.”
clicks.tip: Watch the second terminal: in flight climbs into the hundreds, retries pour in. Fallback: results/switched-big-1.html.

clicks.say: “The small sale, faint, for reference.”

Plays the big sale and freezes. “p99: 2,325 milliseconds. 939 payments failed. 829 reservations in flight at once. Nothing crashed. No exception you would notice. It just stopped working for a thousand people.”
clicks.tip: Stop talking for two seconds after the freeze.
clicks.more: Across three runs p99 was 2.3 to 3.7 seconds. Quote the run on screen.

clicks.say: “The same sale as a picture. This is a simulation, calibrated to the recorded run: it reads 829 in flight at the same moment the real run did. Traffic on the left, the reservations in flight in the middle, the 20 connections, the provider.”

Plays three seconds, then freezes. “700 a second. Nothing makes anyone wait at the door, so they all go straight to the pool and the provider. 829 in flight. The red ones have already missed half a second. The provider is full and refusing charges.”
Plays on. “When the sale ends it drains in about three seconds.”
“The totals: 939 payments failed, 4,000 retries, and 9,061 seat holds had to queue for a connection.”

why.goal: Explain why this never happened before the switch.

clicks.say: “Why didn’t this happen before? Sixteen platform threads meant at most sixteen seat holds and payments at once. Nobody designed that as protection. It was an accident, but it was a limit.”
“With virtual threads every reservation starts all five calls at once. Parked threads are almost free, so nothing pushes back.”
“The limit moved to the 20 connections and the provider. 829 reservations in flight, waiting on one or the other.”

“Sixteen protected the database and the provider. Nobody wrote it down. And to be fair: sixteen threads would have been worse at this sale, p99 11.7 seconds. They failed slowly, in their own queue, where you could see it.”
“The provider takes 20 at a time. It refused 4,939 charges.”
“Each refusal was retried, up to three times. 4,000 retries, each one more load on a provider that was already full.”
“And 939 customers had their payment fail anyway.”
“That @Retry was always in the code. It never fired before the switch, because sixteen threads never sent more than the provider could take.”
“First check to take home.” Read it out. “If the honest answer used to be ‘the thread pool’, that limit is gone the day you switch.”
“So we rebuild it. Not by going back to sixteen threads. By writing the limits down: a door in front, and a budget behind it for each dependency.”

door-code.goal: Admission control in a Jakarta REST filter.

clicks.say: “The door is a Jakarta REST request filter with a semaphore.”
“The limit comes from config: 24.”
“tryAcquire, not acquire. If there is no room we don’t queue at the door, we answer 503 with Retry-After at once.”
“And the response filter hands the permit back on the way out.”
“Why 24? The provider does about 360 charges a second, and a reservation takes about 52 ms. Little’s law: 360 times 0.052 is about 19 inside at full speed. 24 leaves room for bursts.”

door.goal: The door survives the big sale.

clicks.say: “The same simulation, with the door.”
Plays three seconds, then freezes. “In flight climbs to 24 and stops. Everyone else is turned away at once.”
“926 told to try again at once, never more than 24 inside. But 24 is more than the provider’s 20, so 50 payments still failed. That is the next fix.”

budgets-code.goal: The same attribute, now a budget per dependency.

clicks.say: “Behind the door, one executor per dependency.”
“Seat holds get maxAsync = 20, because the pool has 20 connections.”
“Payments get maxAsync = 20, because the provider takes 20 at a time. Work past the budget waits in our executor, not as a 429.”
“It is the same attribute we deleted. Now it is a budget, not a thread count. Virtual threads stay on.”
clicks.more: @Bulkhead(20) from MicroProfile Fault Tolerance is another way to write the payment budget.

rebuilt.goal: The rebuilt service at the big sale.

clicks.say: “The same launch. The broken run, faint.”
Plays the rebuilt run. “p99: 114 milliseconds. The grey columns are the people told to try again: 991. And not one payment failed.”

result.goal: Refusing some got more served on time.

clicks.say: “Saying no to 991 people got 1,080 more a fast yes.”
“And nobody’s payment failed. A fast no beats a slow yes and a failed charge.”
“Second check.” Read it out. “Sixteen was a number left over from a thread pool. Twenty and twenty came from the dependencies.”
“Part three. The provider has a bad day: 1,800 ms a charge. The customer waits 500.”
“orTimeout on the combined future. At 500 ms the customer gets a 504 and a message to try again.”
“What happens to the payment?”

leak.goal: The customer left. The work stayed.

clicks.say: Plays in real time. Stay silent until it stops. “At 507 ms we told the customer it failed. At 1,850 ms we charged the card.”
“And the customer presses retry. That is a second charge on its way.”
“orTimeout limits how long the customer waits. It says nothing to the work.”

cancel-code.goal: Cancel every part at the deadline.

clicks.say: “The fix: when the deadline fires, cancel every part.”
“One line: part.cancel(true).”
“A detail worth knowing: on Liberty, cancel(true) on a managed CompletableFuture interrupts the task. On a plain JDK CompletableFuture it does nothing to the running task.”

cancel.goal: Cancel stops your call, not the charge.

clicks.say: Plays. “Timed out at 506, payment call cancelled at 507. The last run’s long bar is the ghost.”
“But look at the provider. It already had the request, and it charged the card anyway. Cancel stops your call. It does not un-send the charge.”
clicks.more: Measured: with cancel, the provider still logged one charge.

key.goal: Idempotency keys make the retry safe.

clicks.say: “So the retry has to be safe. The customer sends an Idempotency-Key, and we pass it to the provider.”
“Without a key the retry is a new reservation: two charges, eight seat holds. With the key the retry finds the first charge: 201 in 26 milliseconds, four seat holds.”
“Charged once.”
“Where this is going: structured concurrency. The scope owns the deadline, and nothing leaves the scope while its work runs.”
“It is a preview in JDK 25, and this is plain Java from my last talk, not Liberty yet.”
“Cancelled at 207, reported at 208: the work stops before the customer is told.”
“Third check.” Read it out.

watch-list.goal: The metrics that warn before collapse.

clicks.say: “What to watch. Requests in flight: 829 at the big sale, 24 behind the door.”
“Waits for a connection. Liberty publishes it as a connection-pool metric.”
“Retries. Each one is more load.”
“Refusals: the 429s you get and the 503s you give. The first is a warning, the second is your protection working.”
“And p99 second by second. An average over the run hides a sale.”

checks.goal: Leave them with something to do on Monday.

clicks.say: “Three checks for Monday.” Read them. Leave the slide up for a moment.

jobs.goal: The whole talk in one slide.

clicks.say: “Threads got free. Nothing else did. Sixteen threads were doing three jobs nobody gave them.”
“Keeping the database under its 20 connections.”
“Keeping the provider under its limit, so @Retry never fired.”
“Being the one number in the system that said ‘enough’.”
“Those jobs are yours now.”

thanks.goal: Close, point at the code, open the floor.

clicks.say: “Thank you. The code is on GitHub, and ./run.sh state before, switched, budgeted, deadlines puts every version in front of you.”
“If you want the long version, it is in the book. The QR code goes there.” Then take questions from the chat.

pinning.goal: Backup for questions: pinning was a different problem, and it is fixed.

clicks.say: The top chart plays. “Pinning was this: on JDK 21 a virtual thread waiting inside synchronized held its carrier. Twenty tasks, two carriers, a full second.”
The lower chart plays. “JDK 24 fixed it in JEP 491. The same code on JDK 25: about a tenth of a second.”
“So pinning is fixed, and it is not why our service broke at the big sale. Pinning was the JVM’s problem. The limits are ours.”
